title: Achaemenid Mesopotamia
subtitle: 539–331 BC · The Wealthiest Satrapy of Persia — the Light Hand of Cyrus, the Revolts, the Golden Age of Astronomy, and the Coming of Alexander

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Cyrus's conquest and the light Persian hand, Darius crushing the pretenders on the Behistun cliff, Xerxes ending the title 'King of Babylon', the long Achaemenid peace, and Gaugamela and the entry of Alexander

entries.label: Cyrus and Cambyses — conquest and continuity
entries.hint: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 as, in his own telling, Marduk's chosen deliverer, and changed almost nothing: he kept the title 'King of Babylon, King of the Lands', left the temples, the archives and the administration in place, and installed a governor. His son Cambyses acted as king of Babylon and then conquered Egypt in 525, dying on the road home in 522. The empire's richest province had barely felt the change of master.
entries.note: The Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7); the Cyrus Cylinder; Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002).

entries.label: Darius I and the pretenders on the cliff
entries.hint: In the chaos after Cambyses' death two men in turn declared themselves 'Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus' and seized Babylon; Darius crushed both, and had the whole struggle carved in three languages onto a cliff at Bisitun. He then rebuilt the empire — the fixed satrapies, the annual tribute (Babylonia and Assyria assessed at a thousand talents of silver, the highest), the royal road, the daric coinage, and 'the law of the king'.
entries.note: The Bisitun inscription (Rüdiger Schmitt, ed.); the Babylonian pretenders Nidintu-Bel and Arakha; Briant (2002).

entries.label: Xerxes and the end of 'King of Babylon'
entries.hint: Early in Xerxes' reign two more Babylonian pretenders rose, in 484; he put them down hard. Afterward the kings dropped the separate title 'King of Babylon', the satrapy was merged with Assyria, and the property of the rebel families was confiscated — the point at which the great old civic archives fall silent. A later Greek tradition adds that the Esagila was stripped and Marduk's golden statue melted down, though the cuneiform record does not confirm it.
entries.note: Caroline Waerzeggers, 'The Babylonian Revolts against Xerxes and the "End of Archives"' (AfO 2003/04); the melted-statue tradition in Herodotus I.183 and Strabo XVI.1.5.

entries.label: The long Achaemenid peace
entries.hint: Under Artaxerxes I, Darius II and Artaxerxes II, Babylonia had a century and a half of quiet under distant kings — the imperial treasury and granary, its grain and silver funding the wars in Greece and Egypt, its estates in the hands of the Persian nobility. The Murashu archive of Nippur documents the crown-land system in its middle. The 'revolt of the satraps' in the 360s barely touched the province.
entries.note: Muhammad Dandamayev, 'A Political History of the Achaemenid Empire' (1989); Matthew Stolper, 'Entrepreneurs and Empire: The Murashu Archive' (1985).

entries.label: Artaxerxes III, Darius III and the fall
entries.hint: Artaxerxes III reconquered a long-lost Egypt in 343 with great brutality, and the empire seemed restored. His successor Darius III then faced Alexander. On 1 October 331 the two armies met on the plain of Gaugamela, within sight of the ruins of Nineveh; the Persian line broke, Darius fled the field, and the following year his own satrap Bessus murdered him. The Achaemenid Empire was over.
entries.note: Arrian, 'Anabasis' III.8–16; the 'Astronomical Diary' for 331 BC (Sachs & Hunger); Briant (2002).

entries.label: Alexander enters Babylon
entries.hint: Three weeks after Gaugamela, the satrap Mazaeus surrendered Babylon and Alexander entered in state. On the advice of the Chaldean priests he sacrificed to Marduk and ordered the Esagila and the ziggurat rebuilt — the rubble-clearing alone reckoned at two months' work for ten thousand men, and never finished. He meant Babylon to be the capital of his world empire, and he came back to it to die, in the Southern Palace, in June 323.
entries.note: Arrian, 'Anabasis' III.16 and VII.17; the surrender of Babylon in the Diary for 331; Strabo XVI.1.5 on the ziggurat.

entries.label: The satrapy of 'Babylonia and Across-the-River'
entries.hint: Under Cyrus and Cambyses a single vast satrapy ran from the Zagros to the border of Egypt; Darius left it whole, and Xerxes finally split it. The satrap — a Persian noble at Babylon, one of the empire's most powerful officers — held the tribute, the garrison and the courts, with a royal 'overseer' planted in each great temple. The chancery worked in Aramaic. Babylon was one of the four cities the Great King used as a residence.
entries.note: Amélie Kuhrt, 'The Persian Empire: A Corpus of Sources' (2007); the satrapy structure in Briant (2002).

entries.label: The Persian nobility and the new landholding
entries.hint: Huge tracts of the best Babylonian land passed to the crown, the queen mother Parysatis, the 'king's son', and the Persian grandees, farmed by dependent labour and by soldier-tenants who held plots — the 'bow', 'horse' and 'chariot' lands — in return for military service. Many of the tenants were deportees or the descendants of deportees. The Murashu firm of Nippur made its living managing these estates and equipping these colonists.
entries.note: Matthew Stolper, 'Entrepreneurs and Empire' (1985); Guillaume Cardascia, 'Les archives des Murašû' (1951).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The conquest of 539 and the revolts of the pretenders, the 484 rising and the breaking of the old elite, Babylonia's part in the empire's wars and the March of the Ten Thousand, and the fall at Gaugamela

entries.label: The taking of Babylon and the pretenders' revolts
entries.hint: Cyrus's army broke the Babylonians at Opis in 539 and walked into the city days later. Then, in the succession crisis of 522–521, two Babylonians in turn claimed descent from Nabonidus and held the city for months each before Darius's generals defeated and impaled them. The conquest was easy; keeping the throne of Babylon quiet was not.
entries.note: The Nabonidus Chronicle; the Bisitun inscription on Nidintu-Bel and Arakha.

entries.label: The rising of 484 and the breaking of the elite
entries.hint: Two pretenders, Bel-shimanni and Shamash-eriba, seized the northern Babylonian cities early in Xerxes' reign. The suppression was thorough, and it was followed by a purge: the property of the families that had joined the revolt was confiscated, and the great civic archives of Babylon and Borsippa — the Egibi among them — stop within a year or two. It is the moment the old Babylonian urban aristocracy is destroyed as a class.
entries.note: Caroline Waerzeggers, 'The Babylonian Revolts against Xerxes and the "End of Archives"' (AfO 2003/04).

entries.label: Babylonia in the empire's wars
entries.hint: Babylonian silver, grain and levies fed the empire's campaigns — Xerxes' invasion of Greece, the long reconquests of Egypt, the subsidies that paid Sparta's fleet in the Peloponnesian War. In 401 the fighting reached Babylonia itself: Cyrus the Younger's revolt against his brother the king was decided at Cunaxa, a day's march from Babylon, and the ten thousand Greek mercenaries he had hired then marched home up the Tigris, past the deserted ruins of Assyria.
entries.note: Xenophon, 'Anabasis' I–III; the Babylonian contribution to the empire's finance in Briant (2002).

entries.label: The revolt of the satraps and the reconquest of Egypt
entries.hint: The western satraps were in near-permanent rebellion through the 360s, and Egypt held its independence for sixty years. Artaxerxes III finally crushed the satraps and, in 343, reconquered Egypt with a savagery the sources dwell on — temples plundered, the sacred Apis bull killed. Babylonia, the loyal centre, funded and supplied all of it and was barely disturbed.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus XV–XVI; Briant (2002), on the 'Great Satraps' Revolt' and the second Egyptian reconquest.

entries.label: Gaugamela and the end of the Achaemenids
entries.hint: Darius III chose the plain near Arbela, cleared and levelled for his chariots, and fielded an army drawn from the whole empire. Alexander's oblique advance drew a gap in the Persian line and drove for the king; Darius fled, and with him the battle. Within a month Babylon had opened its gates; within a year the Persian capitals had fallen; within two, Darius was dead and Alexander was Great King.
entries.note: Arrian, 'Anabasis' III.8–16; the Astronomical Diary for 331 BC records the battle and the panic in Babylon.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The satrapy and the fixed thousand-talent tribute, the temples kept intact under a royal overseer, the confiscation that ended the traditional archives, the Aramaic chancery and the coming of coinage, and the military colony

entries.label: The satrapy and the thousand-talent tribute
entries.hint: Darius fixed the empire's provinces and their dues. Babylonia and Assyria together were the ninth and richest district, assessed at a thousand talents of silver a year plus five hundred castrated boys, and — on Herodotus's reckoning — supplying roughly a third of the whole empire's silver revenue. The assessment was farmed out for collection, and the surplus grain was a strategic reserve for the imperial armies.
entries.note: Herodotus III.89–95; Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002).

entries.label: The temples kept, under a royal eye
entries.hint: The Persians did not touch the temple institutions. The Esagila, the Eanna and the Ebabbar kept their land, their prebends, their calendar and their scholarship. But the crown planted a 'royal overseer' in each to audit and to tax, and laid labour and military obligations on the temple's dependants. It was religious tolerance as efficient administration — leave the machinery running and skim it.
entries.note: Kristin Kleber, 'Tempel und Palast: Die Beziehungen zwischen dem König und dem Eanna-Tempel im spätbabylonischen Uruk' (2008).

entries.label: The end of the traditional archives
entries.hint: The confiscation that followed the 484 revolt broke the old Babylonian civic families. Their private archives — kept for generations, the densest documentation of any ancient society — stop within a year or two, and a new set of families, some of them collaborators, takes their place. The 'long sixth century' of exceptional written evidence ends here, and the record of Babylonian life goes suddenly thin.
entries.note: Caroline Waerzeggers, 'The Babylonian Revolts against Xerxes and the "End of Archives"' (AfO 2003/04); Michael Jursa, 'Aspects of the Economic History of Babylonia' (2010).

entries.label: The Aramaic chancery and the coming of the coin
entries.hint: The empire ran on Imperial Aramaic, written in ink on parchment — one standard official language from Egypt to India — with Babylonian scribes now bilingual and cuneiform retreating to the temple and the observatory. And Darius's gold daric and silver siglos brought coinage into Babylonia for the first time, though the province went on weighing its silver by the shekel for another century before the coin took over.
entries.note: Holger Gzella, 'A Cultural History of Aramaic' (2015); the coinage in Peter Vargyas, 'A History of Babylonian Prices' (2001).

entries.label: The military colony and the bow-land
entries.hint: The crown settled soldier-tenants on plots graded by the equipment they owed — the 'bow-land', the 'horse-land', the 'chariot-land' — held in return for turning out for the king's army or paying a substitute. Many of the colonists were deportees and the descendants of deportees: Judeans, Carians, Egyptians, 'Cimmerians', organised into collectives. The Murashu tablets show them mortgaging and leasing their plots to raise the cost of their own service.
entries.note: Matthew Stolper, 'Entrepreneurs and Empire' (1985); Ran Zadok on the ethnic groups in the Murashu texts.

entries.label: The satrap's court and the great estates
entries.hint: The Persian aristocracy held vast Babylonian estates — the king's, the queen mother Parysatis's, the 'king's son's' — run by stewards and rent-farmers for owners who lived at court or in Iran. The satrap kept a great household at Babylon, and the Great King himself used the city as one of his four seasonal residences, alongside Persepolis, Susa and Ecbatana. The province's wealth was administered, in large part, by and for people who were not there.
entries.note: Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002); the royal residences in Xenophon, 'Cyropaedia' VIII.6.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The New Year without a king to lead it, the great century of astral science, the Judean community after the return, the Uruk revival of Anu, and the Persian gods in Babylonia

entries.label: The New Year without a king
entries.hint: The akitu festival turned on the king coming before Bel to 'take the hand of Marduk' and be re-invested. The Persian kings were usually elsewhere and did not perform it. After the revolts, the great procession seems to have lapsed or been cut back for long stretches, and the Babylonian scholars recorded the years 'the king did not come, Bel did not go out' as a mark of a broken age.
entries.note: Julye Bidmead, 'The Akitu Festival' (2002); the 'Bel did not go out' notices in the Babylonian chronicles.

entries.label: The great century of astronomy
entries.hint: Under the Achaemenids Babylonian astronomy reached its mature form: the twelve-sign zodiac standardised, the arithmetical lunar and planetary theories worked out — the Greeks later credited named Babylonians, 'Naburianos' and 'Kidenas', with them — the 'Goal-Year' method for reusing old data, and the personal horoscope. The temple scholars of the Esagila and the Bit Resh were, without any competition anywhere, the world's astronomers.
entries.note: Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004); the named astronomers Nabu-rimanni and Kidinnu in Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975).

entries.label: The Judean community after the return
entries.hint: When Cyrus allowed it, a minority of the exiles went back to Jerusalem, rebuilt the Temple by 516 and the walls under Nehemiah about 445, and produced the books of the Persian period — Ezra-Nehemiah, Chronicles, Haggai, Zechariah. But most Judeans stayed in Babylonia. That community persisted, farming and trading around Nippur and Babylon, and over the following centuries became the largest and most learned Jewish population in the world.
entries.note: Rainer Albertz, 'Israel in Exile' (2003); the stay-behind community in Laurie Pearce & Cornelia Wunsch, 'Documents of Judean Exiles' (2014).

entries.label: The Uruk revival of Anu
entries.hint: As Babylon's Esagila declined, Uruk went the other way. Its temples were rebuilt, a distinct local scholarly tradition flourished, and — in a deliberate assertion of the city's own identity — the sky-god Anu was promoted over Inanna-Ishtar as Uruk's chief deity, with a rebuilt temple, the Bit Resh, and a reworked theology to match. It was religious localism as a response to being ruled from far away.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Pantheon of Uruk during the Neo-Babylonian Period' (2003); the Bit Resh and the Anu-Antu cult.

entries.label: The Persian gods in Babylonia
entries.hint: The Persian rulers and settlers brought their own religion — Ahura Mazda invoked in the royal inscriptions, the fire cult, the priestly 'magi', and from Artaxerxes II the promotion of the goddess Anahita. Persian and Babylonian practice coexisted in the province with little visible friction, each in its own sphere. It is the start of the long entanglement of Iranian and Mesopotamian religion that runs through the Parthian and Sasanian centuries.
entries.note: Mary Boyce, 'A History of Zoroastrianism' vol. 2 (1982); the Anahita cult in the Artaxerxes II inscriptions.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Babylonian scholarly tradition under empire and history written as prophecy, Persian imperial art built by Babylonian hands, the triumph of Aramaic and the alphabet, and the trilingual cliff that unlocked cuneiform

entries.label: The scholarly tradition holds
entries.hint: As Aramaic took over daily life, cuneiform learning contracted to the temple libraries of Babylon, Borsippa and Uruk — and there it went on, copying and commenting on the omen series, the epics, the lexical lists and the rituals, and generating the astronomical texts that were its living frontier. It is a narrower world than the Sargonid one, but continuous: an unbroken written tradition now more than two thousand years deep.
entries.note: Philippe Clancier, 'Les bibliothèques en Babylonie dans la deuxième moitié du 1er millénaire av. J.-C.' (2009); Eleanor Robson, 'Ancient Knowledge Networks' (2019).

entries.label: Persian art built by Babylonian hands
entries.loc: Found: Susa · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: The 'Achaemenid' court style drew directly on Mesopotamian models, and often on Mesopotamian workers. Darius's foundation charter for his palace at Susa names the Babylonian brickmakers who made its glazed-brick friezes of archers and lions, the timber quarried in Assyria, the goldsmiths of Media and Egypt. The winged-bull column capital is the lamassu re-used. The empire's new imperial art was, in its craft, the old one continued.
entries.note: The Susa foundation charter of Darius (DSf); Margaret Cool Root, 'The King and Kingship in Achaemenid Art' (1979); the 'Archers frieze' in the Louvre.

entries.label: The triumph of Aramaic and the alphabet
entries.hint: Imperial Aramaic, written in the alphabet on parchment and papyrus, was now the language of administration, of law, of literature and of the street, from the Nile to the Indus. The Ahiqar story circulated in it; the documentary habit of the whole Near East was Aramaic. Cuneiform, and Akkadian, survived — but as the specialist scripts of the temple and the observatory, no longer the way the region wrote to itself.
entries.note: Holger Gzella, 'A Cultural History of Aramaic' (2015); the Aramaic Ahiqar papyrus from Elephantine (5th century).

entries.label: The trilingual cliff at Behistun
entries.loc: Behistun (Bisitun), on the road to Ecbatana
entries.hint: Darius had his victory over the 'liar kings' — including the two Babylonian pretenders — carved a hundred metres up a cliff face in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, with a relief of the king and the bound rebels. Copies in Aramaic were circulated across the empire. And because it was trilingual, it became, in the 1840s and 1850s, the bilingual key by which Henry Rawlinson and others deciphered cuneiform — opening the entire Mesopotamian written record.
entries.note: The Bisitun inscription (Rüdiger Schmitt, ed., 1991); the decipherment in Kevin Cathcart, 'The Earliest Contributions to the Decipherment of Sumerian and Akkadian' (2011).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Mathematical astronomy in its mature form, the transmission of the zodiac and the sexagesimal degree to Greece, the astrological worldview, and history disguised as prediction

entries.label: Mathematical astronomy in its mature form
entries.hint: By the fourth century the Babylonian astronomers had a complete predictive system: pre-computed tables — ephemerides — giving a body's position month by month, generated from arithmetical 'zigzag' and 'step' functions, with the procedure texts explaining how. They could forecast an eclipse, a first visibility, a solstice, decades ahead, without observing. It reached this form here and then held it, essentially unchanged, for four hundred years.
entries.note: Otto Neugebauer, 'Astronomical Cuneiform Texts' (1955); Mathieu Ossendrijver, 'Babylonian Mathematical Astronomy: Procedure Texts' (2012).

entries.label: The channel to Greece
entries.hint: Babylonian science flowed west. Greek astronomers from the fifth century used Babylonian eclipse records (Ptolemy's earliest went back to 721 BC); the twelve-sign zodiac, the 360-degree circle and the division of the hour into sixty minutes were Babylonian and became Greek and then universal; the arithmetical methods fed Hipparchus. 'Chaldean' became the Greek word for an astronomer — and, later, for an astrologer.
entries.note: Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975); Francesca Rochberg, 'In the Path of the Moon: Babylonian Celestial Divination and Its Legacy' (2010).

entries.label: The astrological worldview
entries.hint: The personal horoscope — the sky at the moment of a birth, read for a life — was a Babylonian invention of these centuries, and with it came the idea that the parts of the body and the fortunes of a person are governed by the signs and the planets. Carried west by the Greeks and then east again through the Islamic and Indian traditions, this framework became a permanent, near-universal feature of how people understood their place in the cosmos.
entries.note: Francesca Rochberg, 'Babylonian Horoscopes' (1998); the melothesia and its transmission in Rochberg (2010).

entries.label: History written as prophecy
entries.hint: Babylonian scholars under empire developed a genre in which the past is written in the future tense — a 'prophecy' that reviews the reigns from Nabonidus through the Persians as if predicting them, and then breaks into a real prediction of a coming deliverer. The 'Dynastic Prophecy', composed around Alexander's conquest, is the fullest example. It is a way of asserting that the sequence of foreign rulers has a shape and an end, and the form runs on into the apocalyptic literature of Daniel.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Babylonian Historical-Literary Texts' (1975); Matthew Neujahr, 'Predicting the Past in the Ancient Near East' (2012).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The wealthiest satrapy and the imperial granary, the Murashu firm and the estate economy, the slow arrival of coinage, the date-and-canal economy at its peak, and the trade of an imperial hub

entries.label: The wealthiest satrapy
entries.hint: Babylonia was the empire's treasury and its granary. It paid the highest tribute of any province, and Herodotus reckoned it supplied a third of the empire's total silver revenue and could feed the Great King's whole household and army for four months of the year. Its surplus grain was a strategic reserve, moved to wherever the empire was fighting. The province the Persians ruled most lightly was also the one they leaned on most heavily.
entries.note: Herodotus III.89–95, I.192; Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002); Michael Jursa, 'Aspects of the Economic History of Babylonia' (2010).

entries.label: The Murashu firm and the estate economy
entries.hint: The archive of the Murashu of Nippur — some seven hundred tablets over fifty years — shows one firm running the middle of the Achaemenid rural economy: leasing the estates of Persian nobles and the plots of military colonists, advancing seed, plough-teams and cash, collecting rents, paying the colonists' taxes and equipping them for the muster, and keeping a steady margin on all of it. It is the clearest surviving picture of how the whole system was made to pay.
entries.note: Matthew Stolper, 'Entrepreneurs and Empire: The Murashu Archive, the Murashu Firm, and Persian Rule in Babylonia' (1985).

entries.label: Coinage comes slowly
entries.hint: Darius's gold daric and silver siglos circulated in Babylonia, but the province kept weighing its silver by the shekel for most of the period, treating coins as bullion with a maker's guarantee. The prices in the Astronomical Diaries stay in weighed silver throughout. The real shift to a coined economy — struck mints, a money supply, coined wages — is a Hellenistic development, still a century off.
entries.note: Peter Vargyas, 'A History of Babylonian Prices in the First Millennium BC' (2001); Julien Monerie on the Hellenistic transition.

entries.label: The date-and-canal economy at its peak
entries.hint: The Achaemenid peace and the imperial interest in revenue brought southern Babylonian agriculture to a height not reached again until the Abbasid period — new canals, the maintenance of the old ones, a landscape of date orchards and irrigated barley, and a population and a cultivated area at their maximum. The date was food, wealth and money-crop at once, and the estate archives are thick with orchard leases.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981), on the Achaemenid–Seleucid settlement maximum; Jursa (2010).

entries.label: The trade of an imperial hub
entries.hint: Babylon sat on the empire's arteries — the royal road from Sardis to Susa passing close by, the Tigris and Euphrates carrying bulk goods, the Gulf route reaching Arabia and India. Herodotus describes the round hide boats of Armenia floating downriver to the city loaded with wine, breaking up on arrival, and the crews carrying the hides back by donkey. The commercial pivot role of Mesopotamia carried straight on under Persian rule.
entries.note: Herodotus I.194 (the Armenian boats), V.52–54 (the royal road); Briant (2002).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Achaemenid glazed brick carried to Susa and Persepolis, the upkeep of the Babylonian canals as a fiscal asset, and the ephemeris as an abstract scientific tool

entries.label: The glazed brick carried to Susa and Persepolis
entries.hint: When Darius built his palaces at Susa and Persepolis, he brought Babylonian brickmakers and the Babylonian glazed-brick relief with him — the friezes of archers and lions at Susa are their work — and adapted the lamassu into the winged-bull column capital. The Persians also spread the underground water-channel, the qanat, across the empire by granting its builders a long tax exemption. Mesopotamian building technique became imperial technique.
entries.note: The Susa foundation charter (DSf); the qanat policy in Polybius X.28 and Briant (2002).

entries.label: The canals kept up as a fiscal asset
entries.hint: The Persian administration treated the Babylonian irrigation network as revenue infrastructure and kept it in repair — the great feeder canals, the 'King's Canal' linking the rivers, the marsh sluices — laying the dredging and embanking obligations on the temples and the military colonists. A canal system needs constant labour to survive; the Achaemenid century is one of the periods when it was maintained rather than allowed to silt.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the corvée obligations in the Murashu and temple archives.

entries.label: The ephemeris as an abstract tool
entries.hint: The pre-computed astronomical table — the ephemeris — and its instruction sheet, the procedure text, together made prediction portable: any trained scribe could generate the position of the moon or a planet for a future month by running the arithmetic, with no need to observe or to understand a physical model. It is a genuinely abstract scientific technology — a method detached from its maker and transmissible on a clay tablet.
entries.note: Mathieu Ossendrijver, 'Babylonian Mathematical Astronomy: Procedure Texts' (2012).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Babylon as one of the four royal capitals, the channel of Babylonian science to the Greeks, the consolidation of the Judean diaspora, the Persian settlement and the Iranian tie, and Alexander's plan for a Babylonian capital

entries.label: Babylon, a royal capital of the empire
entries.hint: Babylon was one of the four cities the Great King used as a seat — with Persepolis, Susa and Ecbatana — and he commonly wintered there. The satrapal court, the Persian nobility's estates, and the constant traffic of the empire made it a cosmopolitan imperial city: Persians, Judeans, Egyptians, Anatolians, Arabs and, increasingly, Greeks, doing business in Aramaic in the largest city west of India.
entries.note: Xenophon, 'Cyropaedia' VIII.6.22; the winter residence in Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002).

entries.label: The Chaldean channel to the Greek world
entries.hint: The transmission of Babylonian science west ran through people as well as texts. Greek writers consulted 'the Chaldeans'; astronomical records physically travelled; and around 281 BC a Babylonian priest, Berossus, wrote a history of Babylonia in Greek for the Seleucid court — passing the flood story, the king-lists, the cosmology and the astronomy into the Greek stream. The pipeline that carried the zodiac to Europe was open by the Achaemenid period.
entries.note: Amélie Kuhrt, 'Berossus' Babyloniaka and Seleucid Rule in Babylonia' (1987); Geert De Breucker on Berossus.

entries.label: The Judean diaspora consolidates
entries.hint: The return under Cyrus split the Judean people permanently into two centres — the smaller, poorer community that rebuilt Jerusalem, and the larger, wealthier one that stayed in Babylonia. The tension shows in Ezra-Nehemiah's suspicion of those who had not gone. Over the following centuries the Babylonian community became the demographic and, in time, the intellectual heartland of Judaism, a role it held until the coming of Islam.
entries.note: Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora: Jewish Constructs in Late Antiquity' (1997); Rainer Albertz, 'Israel in Exile' (2003).

entries.label: The Persian settlement and the Iranian tie
entries.hint: Persian nobles, soldiers, administrators and their households settled across Babylonia, and Iranian names spread through the Babylonian tablets. It is the beginning of a fusion of the Iranian and Mesopotamian worlds — political, religious and demographic — that deepens under the Parthians and Sasanians and never fully unwinds. Aramaic was the medium that let the two societies interlock.
entries.note: Ran Zadok on Iranian anthroponyms in the Babylonian corpus; Briant (2002).

entries.label: Alexander's plan for a Babylonian capital
entries.hint: Alexander meant Babylon to be the capital of his world empire. He ordered the Esagila and the ziggurat rebuilt, sailed a fleet down the Euphrates, planned a great harbour and an expedition to circumnavigate Arabia, and gathered his army there for it. He died in the Southern Palace in June 323 with the plans unexecuted. The Achaemenid idea of Babylon as an imperial node passed to the Hellenistic kingdoms, and the Seleucids built their own capital, Seleucia, a short way up the Tigris.
entries.note: Arrian, 'Anabasis' VII.17–19; the 'last plans' in Diodorus XVIII.4; Strabo XVI.1.5.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The rich, populous, cultured province ruled from elsewhere, the demographic peak and the mixed population, the Assyrian ruins as a byword for desolation, and the Achaemenid template for a millennium of imperial rule

entries.label: Rich, populous, cultured — and ruled from elsewhere
entries.hint: Achaemenid Babylonia was the paradox at the heart of the empire: its wealthiest province, its granary, its most populous land, and the cultural senior of its Persian masters — and yet governed by a satrap on behalf of a king who lived at Persepolis and Susa. It was the treasury and the intellectual centre of a world it did not rule. That relationship — a courted, taxed, deferred-to Babylonia inside a larger empire — is the shape of the next thousand years.
entries.note: Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002); Caroline Waerzeggers & Maarja Seire (eds.), 'Xerxes and Babylonia' (2018).

entries.label: The demographic peak and the mixed population
entries.hint: Under the long peace the province reached its greatest population and its greatest extent of cultivation before the Islamic period. And its people were varied as never before: Babylonians; the descendants of Assyrian- and Babylonian-era deportees; Judeans; Persian settlers; Arabs along the western fringe; and a growing number of Greeks. What held them together was not a shared origin but a shared language, Aramaic, and a shared master.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the ethnic mix in Ran Zadok's onomastic studies.

entries.label: The Assyrian ruins as a byword
entries.hint: The empty mounds of Nineveh, Kalhu and Assur lay in the northern part of the satrapy. When Xenophon's Ten Thousand marched past them in 401, retreating up the Tigris, they recorded them as the huge deserted walls of a people whose name they did not know — 'Larissa' and 'Mespila'. By the Achaemenid period 'Assyria' was fully a memory, and 'Babylonia' the living name of the whole land.
entries.note: Xenophon, 'Anabasis' III.4.7–12.

entries.label: The Achaemenid model for a millennium
entries.hint: The two Achaemenid centuries settled the form Mesopotamia would take under foreign rule for the next thousand years: the temples and their archives and astronomy left running, the land taxed through a satrap, the administration in Aramaic, a Persian or Greek elite over an Aramaic-speaking majority, and Babylon a great provincial city rather than a capital. The Seleucids, the Parthians and the Sasanians each reproduced the pattern with local variations.
entries.note: Amélie Kuhrt & Susan Sherwin-White, 'From Samarkhand to Sardis: A New Approach to the Seleucid Empire' (1993), on the continuity.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The temple scholar as the last carrier of the written tradition, the military colonist on his bow-land, the Persian estate-holder and his steward, the Judean who stayed, and the dispossessed old family

entries.label: The temple scholar as the last carrier of the tradition
entries.hint: The astronomer-priest of the Esagila kept the nightly Diary, computed the ephemeris, held a temple prebend for the work, and taught the whole craft to his son. Around him the city had shifted to Aramaic and the alphabet; his cuneiform learning was now a specialist inheritance, guarded within a few families. He was, without a rival anywhere, the frontier of exact science — and the tail end of a two-and-a-half-thousand-year written tradition.
entries.note: Philippe Clancier, 'Les bibliothèques en Babylonie' (2009); Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004).

entries.label: The military colonist on his bow-land
entries.hint: A colonist — a Judean, a Carian, an Egyptian, the grandson of a deportee — held a 'bow-land' plot near Nippur in return for turning out for the king's army with a bow, a quiver and a shield, or paying for a substitute. In a bad year he mortgaged the plot to the Murashu to cover the cost of his own service. The obligation and the smallholding both passed to his son. He was the empire's cheap, rooted, hereditary manpower.
entries.note: Matthew Stolper, 'Entrepreneurs and Empire' (1985); the ethnic colonists in Ran Zadok's studies of the Murashu texts.

entries.label: The Persian estate-holder and his steward
entries.hint: A Persian noble, or a member of the royal family, was granted a great Babylonian estate and drew its rent from a distance — resident at the satrapal court or back in Iran, the land run by a local steward or leased to a management firm. The absentee owner and the on-the-ground agent are the two ends of how the province's wealth was actually extracted.
entries.note: Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander' (2002); the estate management in the Murashu archive (Stolper 1985).

entries.label: The Judean who stayed
entries.hint: When Cyrus permitted the return, most Judean families chose Babylonia, where they had land, businesses and two generations of roots. They farmed, traded, lent at interest, kept the sabbath and the festivals, married and named their children, and stayed in touch with the smaller community rebuilding Jerusalem. Over the centuries this was the population that produced the Babylonian Talmud and made itself the centre of the Jewish world.
entries.note: Laurie Pearce & Cornelia Wunsch, 'Documents of Judean Exiles and West Semites in Babylonia' (2014); Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora' (1997).

entries.label: The dispossessed old family
entries.hint: A member of one of the old Babylonian civic houses — a name that ran back centuries in the temple prebends and the land records — joined the 484 revolt, or was near someone who did. Afterward the property was confiscated, the prebends passed to a collaborator, and the archive that had documented the family for six generations simply stops. The failed revolts destroyed the class that had been the bearer of Babylonian civic identity.
entries.note: Caroline Waerzeggers, 'The Babylonian Revolts against Xerxes and the "End of Archives"' (AfO 2003/04).
